own_scenes.family: Soul y proto-funk: Stax, Nueva Orleans, Motown
own_scenes.desc: El soul fue el comienzo de la síntesis de la América negra: el R&B popular con la moral del gospel, el sábado por la noche y el domingo por la mañana en uno. Lo originó en los cincuenta Ray Charles, que convirtió «My Jesus Is All the World to Me» en «I Got a Woman»; Clinton llama a «What’d I Say» el disco más funky jamás hecho. De la iglesia salieron Aretha Franklin, Sam Cooke, Al Green, Johnnie Taylor, Joe Tex, los Staple Singers, Donny Hathaway o Larry Graham. Jerry Wexler dejó a Aretha arreglar sus temas en Muscle Shoals y «Respect» (1967) se volvió la metáfora de los anhelos de todo un pueblo; con ella la reina del soul elevó toda la música negra. El mismo año salió «Cold Sweat», casi el primer groove funk, estallaron los peores disturbios y murieron Otis y Coltrane; los Impressions cantaban «We’re a Winner». Hasta «Say It Loud» (1968) el soul expresó la unidad negra; después vinieron los poetas revolucionarios (Watts Prophets, Gil Scott-Heron, Last Poets) y el black rock.

refs.q: In many ways soul music represented the beginning of the synthesis of black America
refs.para: In many ways soul music represented the beginning of the synthesis of black America—the synthesis of popular R&B styles with the moral overtones of gospel music. Musical barriers were coming down; there was finally empowerment in the unification of the sacred and the secular—Saturday night swing and Sunday morning salvation all in one.

refs.q: What I Say probably got to be the most funky record ever made
refs.para: Charles’s persona was the most convincing aspect of his funky soul style. He was (and is) a living celebration of the soulful, moral, spiritual man, with a sassy, funky, nastay side. His jazzy improvisations took his style beyond the typical R&B fare, and the enthusiasm he brought to the music made it accessible to anyone, and instantly identifiable to black folks. His impact on funk pioneer Maceo Parker was crucial: “What I think I got from Ray Charles was the soul, the sweetness, the depth and meaning of what it was he was doing, which in a sense to me is soul—the feeling of his style.” George Clinton adds that Charles was the original “funky man,” and that his first notions of what was funky came from Ray Charles. “What I Say probably got to be the most funky record ever made—it had to be the epitome … I just didn’t know what I was calling it.”

refs.q: As a metaphor for an entire people’s frustrations and dreams, “Respect” was it.
refs.para: Her first Atlantic album, I Never Loved a Man (1967), was a smash hit, producing perhaps the most important soul song of all time: “Respect.” While the lyrics implied a song about relationships, it nevertheless carried an emotional backlog that symbolized the yearnings of oppressed peoples everywhere. R-E-S-P-E-C-T blew through the spirits of people young and old yearning to be free. As a metaphor for an entire people’s frustrations and dreams, “Respect” was it.

podcast.title: Source of the Amen Break (1969)
podcast.body: The legendary Amen break, a 7-second drum loop recorded by a soul band in 1969, became arguably the most influential rhythmic pattern in modern music. It was widely sampled and became the rhythmic heart of both jungle and drum and bass. "grabado en una carave por una banda de soul el 1969 que acabaría convertiendo en el corazón del jungle y el drama base."

podcast.title: 60s Throwback (1976)
podcast.body: The music for the 1976 film *Sparkle* was a deliberate throwback to the kind of soul music both Curtis Mayfield and Aretha Franklin were recording in the 1960s, resonating particularly with Black audiences. "The music of Sparkle was a deliberate throwback to the kind of Soul both Mayfield and Franklin were recording in the 60s."

podcast.title: Black Music for Black People
podcast.body: During the Black Power movement, soul music was increasingly made by and for African Americans, reflecting the movement's goals of self-determination. Artists like Curtis Mayfield emphasized that the primary intention was to create music for the black community, with crossover success to white audiences being a secondary consideration, if it happened at all. "Curtis Mayfield said that black musicians were making black music for black people and if it crossed over it did. But that was not the point."

podcast.title: Blueprint from "Dance to the Music"
podcast.body: Sly and the Family Stone's hit "Dance to the Music" set a significant blueprint for the sound of soul music that was to emerge and define the early 1970s. "it set the blueprint for the soul and R&B sound that was to follow in the early 70s."

podcast.title: British Youth Culture Appeal
podcast.body: Soul music, alongside R&B, Reggae, and Ska (known as Bluebeat), was embraced by segments of British youth culture like the mods, rockers, and teddy boys, and later by early British punks. "This slightly evolved form of SCAT lived side by side with R&B and Soul and Reggae. It was also embraced by certain segments of British youth culture like the mods and the rockers and the teddy boys."

podcast.title: Building Block in Music
podcast.body: The development of a more gospel-inflected lyric, exemplified by Benny King's "Stand By Me," became a crucial building block in the music that would later be known as Soul. This approach brought the lyrical concerns and style of gospel directly into the secular realm, setting a new trend among black performers. "Another building block in the music that would become known as Soul had been put in place."

podcast.title: Connecting Eras
podcast.body: Jackie Wilson is identified as one of the key links between 1950s R&B and 1960s Soul music. "Someone who inspired Elvis, Michael Jackson, and James Brown, and who provides one of the key links between 50s R and B and 60s Soul."

podcast.title: Decline of a "Brand of Soul"
podcast.body: By the mid-1970s, a particular "brand of soul" music began to fade. Radio programmers perceived it as repetitive, and listeners felt its themes about persistent life problems were no longer resonating as powerfully. This decline coincided with the rise of disco, which offered an escape through dance. "From the perspective of the music, radio programmers thought that if it was getting kind of repetitive and that the people who had been buying it felt like it had more than thin that it was time to move on."

podcast.body: *To Pimp a Butterfly* incorporates deep soul music, which sets it apart from being a mere rap album. This profound integration of soul, alongside jazz and funk, contributes to the album's complex and rich musical texture, showcasing its expansive musical scope. "Val-Soul más profundo."

podcast.title: Evolution of Roy Hammond's Career
podcast.body: Roy Hammond was initially a doo-wop singer in the 1950s before transitioning into a soul singer. His career later expanded to include politically charged funk music, particularly with the release of "Impeached the President" during the Watergate scandal. "Hammond who was a do-up singer in the 50s and a soul singer after that would release a political funk song in the midst of a political scandal is not that unusual"

podcast.title: Influence on Early Rock
podcast.body: Early rock music, particularly its rhythmic and tonal foundations, evolved significantly from soul music and other musical traditions prevalent in the Southern United States during the 1950s. "Venían a evolucionar un poco del sol y venían muy evolucionadas de la música del sur de los Estados Unidos y esos sentó unas bases rítmicas y de tonalidades que se arrastraron durante muchos años."

podcast.title: Influence on MF Doom's Production
podcast.body: Soul music also played a role in shaping MF Doom's production style, contributing to his use of specific rhythmic bases and musical structures. "En la parte de los basses rímpicas, en la parte de productor de música, tiene muchas influencias del jazz, del soul."

podcast.title: Influenced by Billy Ward and The Dominoes
podcast.body: The music that evolved into soul was heavily influenced by groups like Billy Ward and The Dominoes, whose lead singers Clyde McFatter and Jackie Wilson sang in a style that drew extensively from church music. Later, Lieber and Stoller would produce "gospel-infused soul party songs" for the Isley Brothers. "We've talked before about how Billy Ward and the Dominoes were a huge influence on the music that became soal, with hit records like Have Mercy Baby."

podcast.title: Les Paul Guitar's Versatility
podcast.body: The Gibson Les Paul guitar has been continuously in production since its 1952 introduction and is widely used across virtually every genre, including soul. Its solid-body design resolved feedback issues common with older hollow-body guitars, making it ideal for amplified soul music. "The Les Paul has been in production ever since, and has been used by guitars into rock, punk, metal, pop, country, soul, R&B, jazz, reggae, and virtually every other genre you want to mention."

podcast.title: Redefinition in the 1970s
podcast.body: Soul music underwent a significant redefinition in the early 1970s, notably by artists like Isaac Hayes, who expanded its sonic and thematic boundaries. This era saw a shift from previous popular formulas, with artists exploring funkier sounds and more explicit social commentary. "Isaac Hayes... redefined what soul music could be."

podcast.body: Soul music, along with funk and disco, was a primary genre from which early hip hop producers sourced their samples. Artists would extract short fragments from these existing records to create the foundational loops and rhythms of early hip hop tracks. "se basaba en coger de canciones que ya existían, principalmente del sol, del fankey, del musical disco."
